What I regret here is the way that you are interrupting the proceedings at the time that the Prosecutor is conducting his cross-examination, which he can conduct the way he likes. That's all. Please continue, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, Judge Jorda asks at line 20: "JUDGE JORDA: From Colonel Stewart, yes, I understand that, General Blaskic. What I'm asking is you to tell us specifically whether this was the first time that you had heard something spoken about Ahmici and what happened? That was the 22nd of April; is that correct? A Mr. President, there are two questions there, as far as I'm concerned. I first heard Ahmici being mentioned in this letter, but as far as the suffering of civilians is concerned, I first heard about that on the 20th of April, 1993 at the meeting in Zenica ..."

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. Could you please slow down? Now I heard in the interpretation that I was, on the 22nd of April, 1993, at a meeting in Zenica. Never did I say that I was in Zenica at a meeting on the 22nd of April, 1993. This is way too fast, and I'm not in a position to follow what you've been reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, you received a letter from Colonel Stewart on the 22nd of April, 1993. Judge Jorda's question is about that particular point. "JUDGE JORDA: ... What I'm asking you is to tell us specifically whether this was the first time that you had heard something spoken about Ahmici and what happened? That was the 22nd of April; is that correct? A Mr. President, there are two questions there, as far as I'm concerned. I first heard Ahmici being mentioned in this letter ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can our client see the transcript, Mr. President? I know you don't have it in front of you. You can't see that counsel is redacting my client's answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll read the whole portion if we can get through this. I'll read what I just read before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me repeat once again that the witness is big enough to say what he needs to say. I am sorry for having to repeat that, but I am prepared to satisfy you on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "A I first heard Ahmici mentioned in this letter, but as far as the suffering of civilians is concerned, I first heard that on the 20th of April, 1993 at the meeting in Zenica when Dzemo Merdan, in a heated debate got up and said, 'You down there killed civilians.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, did you tell Slavko Marin that civilians had been murdered in Ahmici in your conversation with him on the 20th of April, 1993? Did you or did you not? "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I asked for all reports to be submitted to me in connection with the murdered civilians, that is to say, all the reports that we received on that day and until that day. Possibly I did not specify that area, but when he said, "By the road," then I thought of the places near the road in that village, and it was the unit of the military police that was in that part of the front line near the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So did you mention Ahmici to Marin or did you not? "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not recall having mentioned it to him. I cannot recall at this moment whether I mentioned Ahmici to him or not, but I still state that it is the first time that I specifically heard of the village of Ahmici in Colonel Stewart's letter on the 22nd of April, 1993, that is to say, about the crime and everything else that is mentioned in the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, you did know that the area that Merdan was talking about was by Ahmici; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Merdan, and I'm quoting him now, "You are down here. You killed people down here. Corpses of civilians are in the ditch by the road and about 500 persons were killed." Then I said to him that I suggest that there be a joint commission in order to carry out an investigation and to have a report on all these allegations, and Mr. Ejup Ganic interrupted this discussion and said, I quote: "Let us leave the dead aside. Let us behave responsibly. Let the commanders agree on a cessation of fire, of combat now, and then we will take care of the dead. This has to be stopped," end of quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, do you have any reason to doubt that when Marin says that it was clear in his mind that you told him it was Ahmici, that you, in fact, told him it was Ahmici? Do you have any reason to doubt Brigadier Marin's testimony before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not know what Dzemo Merdan meant, what he thought, because I did not have any opportunity to share views with him on the allegation that he made. But at that meeting, he did not mention the village with a single gesture. I personally understood him to be saying when he said "by the road," that he was referring to all the villages by the road and on the other side of Kuber, when he said "down there."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, I'd like to ask a question. Between the 16th of April at 5.30 in the morning and the 22nd of April, through the letter, you discovered -- give me the letter. You learned from the letter from Colonel Stewart about the massacre in Ahmici. If I've understood correctly, Busovaca Television was aware of what had happened. You were aware that there were combat operations in Ahmici because you were a military leader. Valenta was aware. Cerkez was aware, apparently. Your own chief of staff was aware. Your enemies were aware. Along the road, you were aware. My question therefore is how can you explain that you are the only one, you were the commander in chief of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, were not aware of what had happened? You had a radio which allowed you to receive transmissions, communications. Therefore, you were a chief who was not at all aware of any massacres that had taken place exactly five kilometres along the road from your Vitez headquarters, and you even said this morning to Judge Shahabuddeen that, as the crow flies, you could see the glowing of the fires in Ahmici, and you know that there were military operations being conducted in Ahmici. How can you explain to the Judges militarily that you were not aware of anything, really anything, anything at all? You were the chief who was aware of nothing. You were unaware of everything happening four kilometres from your headquarters. Everybody knows except you. Could you answer the Judges?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can, Your Honour. Mr. President, Colonel Stewart, who wrote this letter to me on the 22nd of April, found out himself on the 22nd about what had happened, although on the 16th of April, he had armoured vehicles, and his vehicles were in Ahmici and his scouts were in Ahmici. I did not have any armoured vehicles, and I was not in a position to leave my command post and to go into that area because then I would have completely neglected my own duty. I did not have a radio communication --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. You had staff meetings every morning. You would gather together with your brigade commanders every morning.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not have a meeting on a single morning. I practically put together three mornings into one single day, as much as my physical abilities allowed me to do so. Fighting was going on. From the 16th of April onwards, there was incessant fighting, including the 20th of April, four days of fighting. I was tied up at my command post. Also, it is not mentioned here what is this that Mr. Valenta knows? I know that there was fighting in Ahmici and I never denied that in this Court, but I don't know that a crime was committed in Ahmici, and that is the core of the matter here. Does Valenta say in his statement -- is he saying that a crime had been committed or does he know that something happened in Ahmici? What is he saying? Further on, I did not have radio communications at any point. I know that there was fighting in Ahmici, and that a crime was committed, that I learned of regrettably only from Colonel Stewart's letter. I wonder how come he didn't know earlier than the 22nd when he had his own soldiers in Ahmici on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, we will find that out when Colonel Stewart comes. That's when we will get the answers. Judge Rodrigues wishes to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I think we already have the answer to that question. One does not need Colonel Stewart to know that on the 16th of April, 1993 a document which we read today, it is Exhibit 690 which says on page 3, I think it's page 3, yes, at 14.15 hours, he refers to Ahmici as having burned houses along with other things along the road. I think that Colonel Stewart already knew by the 16th of April at 14.00 hours, 14.45 I think it was actually. I would like to go back to the question that the President asked you, General Blaskic. You answered several times when the Prosecutor asked you a question that you could not see the fire. I could go a little further back. We also spoke about logistics and we spoke about munitions. What type of munitions, in your opinion, were used to destroy Ahmici? What kind of weapons? What kind of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm going to present my opinion. If we're talking about the type of weapons, it is mostly light infantry arms, that is to say, automatic rifles, and possibly there might have been some smaller calibre anti-armour weapons. As for the type of munitions, infantry weapons use regular bullets and also incendiary bullets. I'm not sure and I do not have information on what was used, but infantry weapons could have used both one and the other; however, when there is fighting in built-up areas, and there was fighting in some 20 built-up areas in Vitez, then it is possible for a regular bullet to cause a fire. For example, if there is dry straw or hay in a shed, even that can put it on fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Was it possible to hear the noise coming from those weapons, the explosions in Vitez or was it not possible?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That morning, the entire town was reverberating with detonations and different explosions in some 20 places, so it was hard to detect what was going on where. It was the easiest to hear the explosions that were directed at the hotel itself. Those I heard very well myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But it was normal to see other people coming in and going out or going back and forth between Vitez and to a place close to Ahmici. Since you were the commander of the Operative Zone, it would be normal to acknowledge that someone gave you the information? It would be completely natural. My question is that -- well, you don't know. You didn't know. That was what Judge Jorda asked you. But I would almost like to ask you the following: You didn't know, but did you want to know?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, certainly. I talked on these two remaining phones, and I cautioned commanders that they should submit to me information on all events, and I asked them to be as precise as possible and for the information to be as timely as possible. But that morning, I did not even have all my co-workers there because they didn't manage to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I am only speaking about this morning, between the 16th and the 17th of April. You had at least two telephones. You were in the basement of the Hotel Vitez, and you had two telephones, at least two of them. Did nobody from outside inform you? Because for your tasks, for your command, it was important to know that.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly, it was important, and I received regular reports and extraordinary reports and reports that I had specifically asked for, and I did receive reports that fighting was going on in Ahmici. However, the problem was that these reports were not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General Blaskic, if, for you and in your opinion, the information was important, on the 22nd of April at least, you noted that all the people hid that information from you, and, therefore, Mario Cerkez knew, Dario Kordic knew, everybody knew, everyone except you. What were your thoughts at the time? If it was important, you were the commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, you knew that all responsibility that happened in Ahmici would fall on you, and you noted that everybody hid the information from you. What were your thoughts at that moment, at that very moment?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, at that moment, then, I did not believe that all these people were concealing this information from me. I did not hold that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: That was true. You realised that all of those people were hiding that information from you. What were your thoughts at that time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, I only established that I was receiving false reports from the commander of the 4th Battalion of the military police and that he had not submitted correct information to me. Until this present day, I do not know whether Valenta, Cerkez, and Kordic had such information about what was mentioned a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, but we already know that. We have the conclusion, and you have the same conclusion as well, that those people, that is, your colleagues, hid that information from you. Let us start with that hypothesis. What were the conclusions you drew? What were your thoughts about that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If you are referring to my immediate associates, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I'm speaking about you; I'm thinking about you. What did you think? What lesson could you draw from those facts, from those conclusions, from those observations?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I didn't understand this right, but the way I understand you is that I came to the conclusion that the commander of the 4th Battalion concealed information from me that he was aware of. Not at any moment did I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: What about Mario Cerkez --

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: -- did he hide the information from you? What about Dario Kordic, did he hide information from you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what he knew. I don't know what he knew, but I'm convinced that Mario Cerkez did not hide information before me. He knew about the fighting, I knew about combat operations, but about the crime, there is an essential difference here. Until this present day, I don't know that Mario Cerkez knew that and that he concealed it from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But, General, I think I have to go back. At least by the 22nd or on the 22nd of April you noted that there were many people inter alia who knew about the crime and they hid that information from you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 22nd of April, Your Honour, I became conscious of the fact that the commander of the 4th Battalion had been sending false reports to me. My associates in the command had all the reports that they received, and they were all unified into one list. From those reports and the operative diary, I never received information similar to the information that Colonel Stewart got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Perhaps we'll go back to that question later, but I think that there is a doubt which has to be dispelled. I think, for the time being, that's all we'll say about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Rodrigues. Mr. Kehoe, let me remind you we have not yet reached the 22nd of April, we're still on the 19th of April. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Actually, we're at the 20th at this juncture. The conversation between Marin and Blaskic was the evening of the 20th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That's right, the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, just using your own logic, you assumed that when Merdan stood up at this meeting in Zenica and told you about these 500 people killed by the ditch, you assumed that that was the ditch near Ahmici, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He said that they were lying alongside the road in the ditch, and the ditch passes both through Ahmici, Nadioci, Santici, and I assumed that it was that main road that was in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well now, on the 21st of April, knowing or assuming that these bodies are lying in that ditch, did you call Pasko Ljubicic on the phone, bring him into your office or talk to him on the phone and say "Pasko, what happened down there?" Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not do that, but I asked Slavko Marin to collect all the reports, to unify them, and to check and see whether we had information of that kind, because I was surprised that through that assertion of Dzemo Merdan in Zenica that this had been passed over and that nobody had reacted to something of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, the one person that could provide you the most information, the one commander that could provide you the most information was Pasko Ljubicic, concerning the activities around Ahmici; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Quite certainly, but he should have given me that kind of information on the 16th, 17th, 18th, and 19th already. If he had been supplying me with false information up until then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine, General. Yet you, on the 21st of April, after hearing about the massacre of civilians, don't try to call or meet the most important commander that could tell you about what happened in Ahmici; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is not right, because he told me what happened up until the 20th and even up to the 22nd, if you will. His reports were signed and clearly testify to the fact that he was not telling me the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, you came back from this meeting on the 20th of April, 1993. On the 21st of April or up until you received the letter from General Stewart on the 22nd, did you make any effort to contact Pasko Ljubicic and ask him what he knew about these dead civilians in Ahmici, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I could not ask him what he knew about the dead civilians in Ahmici because nobody specified them. What was specified was civilians along the roadside. I gave instructions that all reports should be collected together and that they should be preliminarily studied to see whether we had reports of that kind in our operational reports. On the 21st, in the morning, I was at the meeting in Vitez chaired by the UN

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the answer is you never bothered to ask Pasko Ljubicic one question on the 21st or the 22nd until you receive Stewart's letter about these dead bodies down in the ditch by that road. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have said and told you what measures I took, and it was not specifically stated that it was the village of Ahmici until I had received Colonel Stewart's letter. Once I had received that letter, I became conscious that all the reports were incorrect, that is to say, that they were false.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you assumed that the village was Ahmici, didn't you, General, because in response to a question by Judge Shahabuddeen, when Judge Shahabuddeen was talking to you about what Merdan said, you noted on page 18930, he said: "A 'Look, you have killed hundreds of people down there. There are civilians there too in the ditch by the road. There are 500 people who were killed,' and he sat down." Judge Shahabuddeen asked you where was the ditch of which he was speaking, and your answer was: "A I assumed that this might have been in the area of Ahmici."

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, in the area along the roadside. The whole road which goes from Ahmici, Santici, Sivrino Selo, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, let me move to another point. When you got this information from Merdan on the evening of the 20th, did you bother to go down to the area by the ditch on the 21st to find out what had happened, if there were bodies down there, if civilians had been killed? Did you bother to do that or did you send anybody down there to do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I returned late at night, at 23.00 or something of that kind. I was returned by the UNPROFOR vehicles, in the same way that I was transported by UNPROFOR. Then the focus of our activities was to halt combat activities. Had I been able to, I would certainly have toured the area. However, it was very difficult to affect a ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you saying that the area was inaccessible to you and other members of your staff or other members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I'm saying that at that time, in view of the circumstances under which I was functioning and the possibilities of communication, priority was given to achieving a halt to the shooting, and that was General Morillon's priority and the other people present at the meeting. Already, on the 21st, I had another meeting where these questions were discussed, and the leaders of the BH army and the HVO attended the meeting. Even then, nobody went to Ahmici. They visited Kula in Busovaca, because I believe they did not attach, although they too were present at the meeting in Zenica, they didn't attach any importance to the assertions made by Dzemo Merdan, because they had been passed over in silence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, on the 21st, isn't it a fact that ECMM sent a team down to Ahmici to inspect it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what the European Monitors did on the 21st, but I know full well that at the joint meeting between the chief of the main staff of the BH army and the chief of the main staff of the HVO, a decision was reached to tour the position of Kula at Busovaca and that in no detail was the village of Ahmici mentioned, although Dzemo Merdan was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you an ECMM report, sir. It is from the 21st of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 696.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm interested, Mr. Usher, in part (D) at the bottom. It should be 9(D). It starts with, "During the afternoon."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a Busovaca joint commission report of the 29th of April, 1993, excuse me, 21st of April, 1993. The author, cut off, is Major Morsink, now Colonel Morsink. "(D) During the afternoon, the team and ICRC went on their own coordinated mission. The team investigated in (1) Ahmici west - All Muslims gone and in prison in Dubravica. (2) Ahmici east - 90 per cent of all houses as well as the mosque destroyed. No people left. One dead body in a garage 15 metres south-east of mosque. Reported to the local authority. (3) Novaci - Approximately 200 Muslim women and children living in three houses. Half of them would like to be evacuated. (4) Rijeka - A few Muslim families, NTR. (5) Grbavica - A few Croat families. One family would like to be evacuated. ICRC and UNHCR responsible representatives," I suppose, "informed of above-mentioned." Now, these teams, General, include -- or the ECMM team for the Busovaca joint commission, those teams include HVO representatives, don't they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the European Monitoring Mission, the information that you're asking me about, it was not sent to me by the representatives, although I attended the meeting of the 21st. I know about the joint commission for Busovaca dating back to 1993, January 1993, with the members of the HVO and Bosnia-Herzegovina, which took part in the work of that commission. On the 21st of April, 1993, I think that a joint commission was set up on that particular day for Vitez. I do not have information that the commission spent any time in Ahmici or do I have the information that you have just read out to me. I'm hearing this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, do you know that a member of the HVO, Boro Jozic, went with this Busovaca joint commission team for this inspection of Ahmici on the 21st?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I had no knowledge of that up until today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, let us go back to what you did. You did not bother sending anyone over to the Ahmici area to find out whether or not the killings of civilians, as alleged by Merdan, was true, did you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is not true. I received that information with a certain amount of reservation because all the officials at the meeting asked to stop this information. Merdan did not continue to react. That was the only time that Merdan reacted. After the discussion of Ljubo Ganic, everybody agreed that we focus on halting the hostilities. Apart from that, in my own command, I had far fewer associates at that time because two of my associates had already been wounded, Pilicic and Prskalo. Had my proposal been adopted on the occasion that a joint commission check Merdan's assertion, then I would have undertaken the tour, and had the ceasefire been achieved as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did you take Merdan's allegations seriously? Do you think they were serious allegations?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that he overemphasised the number -- exaggerated the number of casualties but I did take what he said seriously. I did take what Merdan said seriously, even if he did not repeat his allegation. As soon as I returned, I asked that all information that came into the command of the Operative Zone be checked out to ascertain whether there would be any information to bear out Dzemo Merdan's allegation. I had no information from the command which would go to support this assertion by Dzemo Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the fact is, General, that you never sent anybody specifically down to that area to see if what Merdan was saying was true in any respect.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Under those conditions, I wasn't in a position to send anybody to the area. I had commanders in the area who informed me about all the goings on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, who ordered the bodies to be started to be cleaned up on the 21st of April in the village of Ahmici? Who ordered that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 21st, is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 21st of April. Who in the HVO ordered that bodies, dead bodies, be picked up in Ahmici, given the fact that you had received these allegations from Merdan on the night of the 20th?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not issue an order of that kind and I don't know that any such order was issued. I know there was an order that the civil protection should see to the area, and that was on the basis of an order from General Petkovic and General Halilovic. This clearing up was on both sides, and this was performed by the civil protection units. Civil protection receives orders exclusively from the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, led me read you the testimony of Witness K, who recounts the picking up of bodies in Ahmici on the 21st. At 4191: "A On the 21st we heard some strange noise. We saw personnel carriers, the U.N. ones, which came up from the main road and stopped in front of the mosque in Ahmici. We saw some U.N. soldiers climbing out of these personnel carriers and as we were observing, we saw that there were three men who approached the house where we were staying. They had blue uniforms and they had gas masks on their heads. We were in this house and one of these men entered the kitchen. The other one went upstairs and the third stayed behind. We pulled back further under that staircase. They went through the house and then they came out. We thought that they were UNPROFOR and we started to come out. My father went out first, and then my uncle, and then myself. Father said, 'People, do not be afraid. We will not do anything to you,' and then one of those men in the blue uniforms jumped up. He was startled and he said, 'Jesus Christ. We're looking for the dead ones and there are still some alive.'" Turning to the next page, 4192: "A The one standing next to him waved, and I noticed from the house that the two soldiers were running up the road, one in a camouflage uniform and one in a black uniform. Then the curses started immediately. They cursed our Balija mothers and they said, 'Kill,' but the man who said 'Jesus Christ,' he said, 'Take these men up in front of the command.' So we started from there and they took us up there. We had to put our hands behind our heads and we had to look down. Q Let me stop you there, Witness K. Did you notice any insignia on the uniform of either the soldier in black uniform or the soldier in the camouflage uniform? A On the black uniform I only saw the word 'Joker' embroidered. I do not know which arm. Q At this point had you concluded that, these soldiers and the men dressed in blue, with the gas masks, were not with UNPROFOR? A Yes. We concluded that these men were not UNPROFOR. Q When you went outside, and they took you outside and you said you had to put your hands on your head, did you see any bodies, any dead bodies? A I saw a body by the gate leading up to the house. It was like a skeleton. It was all burnt out, singed below the knees. It was more singed than burnt, this body. I noticed shoes on the body's feet, the same kind of shoes that our neighbour from number 7 owned. Q Witness K, you said you recognised it by the shoes and that the body was singed. Did you think that the body had been dumped there or the body had been burnt there? A It was dumped there because you could not see any grass that burnt around the body, and we had also heard some voices beforehand, something to the effect that this body was dumped there. Q Earlier, had one of these men told you that they were looking for the dead bodies? A He said, when he said, 'Jesus Christ, we were looking for the dead ones and there are still some live ones here.'" Now, General, the individuals that are dressed in the blue uniforms, those are the Civil Defence people who were assigned to the body pick-up; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that the members of the Civil Defence wore blue uniforms, but I know that I did not issue orders to the Civil Defence to collect dead bodies, and I believe that nobody from my command did so. I do know of one operation to clear up the battlefield. I think it was on the 28th or the 29th of April, on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, would you agree that somebody in the HVO command had to order the Civil Defence to go clean up these bodies in Ahmici? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Civil Defence orders are issued by the civilian authorities to the Civil Defence, so I don't see how that could have happened. I know for certain that nobody from my command issued any command of that kind, nor did I issue an order of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, this was the day after your meeting with Merdan in Zenica; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The date corresponds, but I underline that I hear about that order of the 21st of April, 1993 for the first time. I never issued an order like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us turn to the 22nd and the meeting of the Busovaca joint commission where Major Morsink disclosed before the joint commission what he saw in Ahmici. Now, your representative to the Busovaca joint commission was Franjo Nakic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Franjo Nakic was a member of the joint commission, together with Dzemo Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did Franjo Nakic come back to the Hotel Vitez on the morning of the 22nd and tell you what Major Morsink had discussed and what he had seen in Ahmici the previous day? Did Nakic tell you that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall Nakic coming back. Usually every morning he would go to work with the joint commission and would stay there until late at night, but I'll take a look at my chronology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, you can look at that at the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, as opposed to taking the time, we will hold the question in abeyance and let the witness look at it during the break so that it doesn't take up court time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. You can look for it during the break and then answer the question. Move to the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, the fact of the matter is that you knew exactly what happened in Ahmici well prior to receiving the letter from Stewart on the 22nd; isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have to ask questions, not make assertions. If we're beginning with an assertion, you have to follow it up with a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, you knew prior to receiving Stewart's letter exactly what happened in Ahmici and that civilians and citizens had been massacred there; isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The fact of the matter is, sir, that any number of individuals around you knew, and according to your testimony, you are the only person who didn't; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already said that I knew about the information that I received from my direct subordinates and the information that was recorded in my operative diary, that is to say, the diary of the command. Perhaps individuals --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's not the question, General Blaskic. That was not the question. The question was whether all the people who were named to you and had responsibilities, whether they were political individuals or subordinates or superiors, seemed, I repeat, "seemed," we don't know, but seemed to know certain things that you apparently, and I repeat, "apparently," did not know. I think that's the question.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is not how I understood the question. If that is the question, then I can say that I believe that the members of my command who were together with me in the basement of the hotel quite certainly did not have information that they would hide from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Then rephrase the question. It's a very important question, Mr. Prosecutor. It has to do with knowing whether you were in a command position and could, therefore, know certain things or if you were a commander who, in the end, between those units directly subordinated to -- civilian units and units that received their orders from Mostar, that's the military police, and the politicians, because you weren't involved in politics, that was for the politicians. As far as the civilians go, no, because they were civilian authorities and you were a military person, and between the point you were a military person and this point, you were taking care of the front with the Serbs. Do you accept that you could not know a certain number of things that all those people around you knew? That's the question. I think it's a very simple one.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can only accept that certain individuals outside my command perhaps, that is to say, some of them in the field. For example, we heard testimony from, I think it was, Dr. Mujezinovic who was able to talk to the people living there, living in the village of Ahmici and got information there, and he got information only on the 19th. But I was not in a position to talk to anybody because I was in the basement throughout that time and I was in command down there. So I had to rely on reports from my associates, and I believe that my closest associates knew nothing more than I did myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move to another topic, General, and let me show you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't know if you want to take a break now, as I move to another topic, Mr. President, but anything that Your Honour sees fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. We will take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume now. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I checked in my chronology, and I established that on the 22nd of April, in the morning, I met with Mr. Nakic. After that meeting, he went to the meeting of the joint commission, and I had my next meeting with Nakic only on the 23rd of April, 1993, that is to say, after he finished his work in the joint commission, I believe he went home to rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If the witness can be given Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/56, 456/57, and 456/48.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, taking a look at this first exhibit, which is Stewart's letter to you of the 22nd of April, 1993 concerning the atrocities in Ahmici, General, when you received this letter and you examined it, did you believe what Stewart was telling you was true?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I received this letter, I believed these allegations and I thought they were true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, your response to this letter is contained in 456/57 where you note in the opening line of number 1: "I am ready to send immediately the investigating commission to the village of Ahmici." Now, General, what investigating commission are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm talking about the joint commission that had visited all the contested places until then and where my representatives were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you are talking about the Busovaca joint commission; is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The joint commission from Busovaca, should I say this once again, was established at the meeting on the 20th or the 21st of April. That's the joint commission I'm talking about where my representatives were, Nakic and his associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, did you ever request that joint commission, the Busovaca joint commission, to conduct an investigation of Ahmici? Did you ever request that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From my letter of the 23rd of April, it is quite clear that I am referring to the joint commission, and I wish to send them to carry out an investigation. The practice until then was that all contested places where crimes occurred were to be resolved by the joint commission. On the joint commission were certain officials of the security service on behalf of the HVO and I believe security officials from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina too. For example, such a joint commission went to the village of Katici as well and carried out an investigation when the hostages were taken. I think that it visited Dusina, Lasva, Visnjica, and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did Colonel Stewart understand you to be talking about the Busovaca joint commission when you wrote this letter to him on the 23rd and when you met him on the 24th of April?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that he understood it because this commission could only have been taken care of by his own people, and they were the only ones who could have driven them there too. He was also present at meetings, and he probably knew what the thesis for the "joint commission" were. At the meeting on the 4th of May, I was quite clear, and I also told him what the composition of the joint commission should have been like too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let's look back again at Exhibit 695, which is again Colonel Stewart's diary from the 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Usher, if we could refocus it on page 2, that last paragraph that we chatted about this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let me read you this paragraph that is now on the ELMO: "When lunch was over, I took the ambassadors into Vitez and there met with Valentin and Blaskic. I stated that nothing had happened about a Commission of Enquiry into Ahmici for 18 days, that nobody was charged or arrested to my knowledge and that I knew the names of men accused -- which I would give to the ECMM ambassadors ..." Colonel Stewart is looking for you to set up an investigating commission, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it wasn't that way. At the meeting that I was invited to, I requested, when I took part in the discussion, from Colonel Stewart and from the chairman, Mr. Thebault, that a joint commission be set up. I explained my point of view, saying that that was the only way in which the results of the investigation could be acceptable and that the investigation itself be comprehensive and full. When I was asked how I see the composition of this joint commission, then I explained what I thought the composition of this joint commission should be like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, did you ever instruct any of your representatives or did you yourself go to the Busovaca joint commission meetings, which were held daily, and ask them to conduct an investigation of Ahmici? If you did, tell us when and who made that request.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I composed an answer to the letter, and it was quite clear to Colonel Stewart on the 23rd of April, 1993. At the meeting, that is, this document that was here a few minutes ago, the 4th of May, 1993, again I asked two persons in the highest responsibility, that is to say, the chief of the European Mission, Mr. Thebault, and Colonel Stewart, that a joint commission be set up and that this joint commission carry out an investigation. On the 24th of April, I ordered the security service to start an investigation, because after the meeting with Colonel Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt you, sir, because my question has to do with the Busovaca joint commission that met on a daily basis. My question with regard to those meetings is: Did you ever instruct your representative Nakic or anyone else from the HVO to go to those meetings and request an investigation of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let me check this in my chronology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please, General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am trying to check on my meeting with Mr. Franjo Nakic on the 23rd of April. I know that I was together with him, and I know that already on the 22nd, I presented my point of view to my associates, that I would ask for a joint commission and for a joint investigation, that I would ask that international institutions take part in the investigation. Now I'm just trying to check whether this was on the 23rd exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: While the witness is looking for something, who called together that joint commission?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As the witness noted, there were the weekly meetings of the Busovaca joint commission that had started and had been ongoing for some time. There were some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: These particular meetings were daily meetings. One of the individuals who, as we saw from some of the films and pictures, presided over them was Major Morsink and others. Mr. Friis-Pedersen, I believe, testified about those meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, this is the question: It seems to me, and you will tell me if I'm wrong, on the 23rd of April, if you decided to send an investigating commission, didn't you think that it would have been necessary in your letter to specify with the words saying, for instance, "I'm ready to set up a commission immediately, and I suggest that we set up a joint commission, which seems most appropriate, for establishing the facts." Don't you think so?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, already from the month of January, that is to say, for four months, they had been working through a joint commission, and this had already become a routine thing, that the joint commission actually investigates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But we're not talking about routine things; we're talking about a crime which, at least theoretically, you had some awareness of, and these are important facts, so important, in fact, that you called for a joint commission to investigate. I don't think that it's self-evident that it was the joint commission. You were not the one who was in charge of that joint commission. You were not the owner, as it were, of that joint commission. You assigned it an investigating role, which it could certainly play, but it seems to me that when one reads the sentence in the French version, I put myself in Colonel Stewart's place, he might legitimately believe that you were going to create an HVO investigating commission at your own initiative, all the more so because you say, thank you, Judge Rodrigues, you say "... send an investigating commission immediately," and you're not the one who sets it up like that, because in that commission, there were people who were your enemies. My question is: Don't you think that when you chose to write that way, you would mislead Colonel Stewart who might think that you were establishing an investigating commission on your side? It isn't self-evident that it was the joint commission, and if that was self-evident for you, it seems to me that I would have written, "I believe, Colonel, that the joint commission would be the most appropriate."

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps I was not precise when I was saying "routine thing." I was not trying to say that crimes were a routine thing. I was trying to say that the work of the joint commission was. We had already had a joint commission that had been established. Of course this was a crime. I was not saying that crime was a routine thing, but the form of work of the joint commission was readily recognisable to all, Colonel Stewart and Mr. Thebault included, and the commander of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. You've given me your answer. Judge Rodrigues would like a clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General Blaskic, you said that in your letter, and I'm reading, you say, "I am prepared, I am ready," that is right away, "to send immediately an investigating commission." That was your answer to General Stewart. You said to your collaborators in the joint commission, "I'm going to ask that an investigation be carried out with the participation of international organisations." You said that you yourself were very moved when you learned that there had been crimes committed in Ahmici. Therefore, you're saying one thing to Colonel Stewart, you're saying something else to your collaborators, but what were you doing? What action did you take? Because, ultimately, you did not have available to you a commission in order to send something to Colonel Stewart immediately.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, until then, that is to say, until this investigation, all investigations were carried out by the joint commission. My officers, who were on the joint commission, worked according to my instructions too. I understood that on the 23rd, in the morning, that I would issue an order to Franjo Nakic, with whom I drafted this letter, that at the joint commission an investigation be started of the case in Ahmici. Until then, it was a routine thing. Whatever was supposed to be investigated, in Busovaca, and I talked about Lasva, Dusina, Visnjica. At least it was this joint commission that went out to the ground and it was UNPROFOR that provided for their safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you. You said to Franjo Nakic, "Ask immediately that an investigation be carried out into Ahmici." That's what I understood. You said to Nakic, "I'm going to ask for an investigation." Did you give the order to Franjo Nakic to ask the commission to carry out an investigation immediately? Did you do that or did you not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is what I was looking for here in my notes and that is what I was looking for in my chronology as well, to know exactly what it was like, but I know when I was writing the letter that I told Nakic that that would be our position, my position. The joint commission should carry out an investigation. He was there with me when I was writing this letter, and now I was looking for this piece of information in the chronology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let us look then just a little bit further on this in sequence. Taking your letter to General Stewart, you note, "I am ready to send the investigating commission to the village of Ahmici." In your note to Kordic, Stojic, and Petkovic, and that's 456/58, you note that Stewart is complaining because no commission has been formed. I'm sure you heard Martin Bell testify that during the press conference on the 27th, you stated that a commission was being set up. On the 4th, Stewart again says that nothing had happened about a commission of enquiry into Ahmici for 18 days. Is it your testimony that the commission that's being discussed is the Busovaca joint commission that's been in existence since February of 1993? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, I have about five questions here, so I'll try to answer them one by one. Document 456/58 is not a comprehensive document, that is to say, that this document does not contain everything that I said to Colonel Stewart and everything that I wrote in the original part, that is to say, vis-à-vis the main staff. Secondly, I asked for a joint commission, and I told Colonel Stewart about that too, that whatever I have to say to him is contained in my answer to his letter. Further on, after this meeting I issued an order to the assistant for security to carry out an investigation, but I still believed that a joint commission would be set up after all and that is why, on the 27th of April, I said that the joint commission would carry out the investigation. I asked at this meeting, both from Thebault and from Mr. Stewart, that a commission for Ahmici be a joint commission after all. They asked me why. I said for the sake of the objectivity of the findings and the comprehensiveness of the investigation. So that the investigation results would be acceptable to the BH army. They have to have their representatives on the commission too, and I need the help of the U.N., and I need the help of the European Mission, and I need the help of the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, your representative on the Busovaca joint commission was Franjo Nakic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ever order Franjo Nakic to go to the daily Busovaca joint commission meetings and request an investigation of Ahmici, and if you did make that request of Nakic, when did you do so?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have to look something up in my chronology. I was with Nakic on the 23rd of April when I wrote this letter to Colonel Stewart, and he was also aware of the contents of the letter then and of my position, that is to say, that I would ask for a joint commission to work on the investigation of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question is this: Did Nakic request an investigation of Ahmici by the Busovaca joint commission, and if he did so, when did he do it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know whether he asked for this joint investigation, but I know that I did in this letter to Colonel Stewart. On the 24th, I realised that it would be difficult to achieve, and I ordered the assistant for security to carry out an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you have any piece of paper, any order, any document that you gave to Franjo Nakic to authorise him to request such an investigation of the Busovaca joint commission, any document to support that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That I gave an order in writing to my own chief of staff? I do. In my war diary, I have the meeting with Nakic recorded on the 23rd in the morning, and that he was present when I talked about the letter and the answer to Colonel Stewart, and I know for sure, on the basis of what we discussed today, that he was aware of the fact that I was asking for a joint commission to investigate, but I did not communicate with my own chief of staff by way of issuing written orders. He is my immediate associate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, let's turn to the document that you discussed before and you refer to 456/58, which is your order of the 24th of April, 1993. Now, during the course of your testimony, you made various references to this order. At page 19077, you noted that: "All my positions were given in writing to the main staff on the 24th of April." On page 19166, you noted that: "Military and political leaders should be in Vitez, and this would give momentum and support to the work of the investigating commission." On 19239, you said: "I sent a letter on the 24th of April and expressed to my superiors my stands including that the highest officials should come to the Vitez region." On 19659 to 60 you noted that: "I believe there is a report in which I asked the supreme commander to visit Vitez in order to support us in conducting the investigation." At 20116, you noted that: "Mate Boban had to be in Vitez today." It refers to making a statement about the crime in Ahmici and receiving support from the top political leadership in terms of carrying out an investigation regarding Ahmici. Now, you also noted during your testimony, at page 20115, and again, you reiterated it today, that this document is not complete. Before we look at the contents of this document, General, take a look at the document itself. If we could put the actual original in your hand on the ELMO as opposed to the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You're speaking about 456 and 458?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm talking about 58, 456/58. I want the Serbo-Croatian copy on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Judges don't have any version here. What are you going to give us, Mr. Registrar? The witness cannot have the English and the Croatian and the Judges don't have any at all. I don't have it in French, I understand. I never do. Well, almost never, but at least I'd like to have the English version for my colleagues and myself, and the witness has the version in Croatian. There you go. Thank you very much. This is a document, let me say this so that everyone understands what is happening, in the public gallery. This is a document from General Blaskic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The minutes of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, let's take a look at this original. You wrote this document, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wrote it down in writing. I did not type it out, I wrote it in my own handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your initials are on page 2 in the lower left-hand side -- excuse me, left-hand side, top left, on page 2. Those are your initials there?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You just noted that it was typed for you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The document was written by hand and then the typist typed it out on a typewriter in the form that you see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, this was typed out in your native language, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: To whom did you address it? Who were the individuals to whom you addressed this letter? The vice-president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the head of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna defence department, and the HVO headquarters chief, who were those three?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The vice-president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was Dario Kordic; the representative of the defence department was Bruno Stojic; the chief of the main staff of the HVO was Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, these are very significant people within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before you sent this letter to them, you were very careful, were you not, to ensure that the contents of this were correct; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I always endeavoured to ascertain whether the contents of a letter were the right ones. Sometimes, depending on the situation, I found myself more or less so, but I always tried to ensure that they were under the given circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you reviewed it before you sent it out to these three very important people?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember. Probably I read through it very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Don't argue, please. Just ask your questions. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you review it before you sent it out, before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say now because it was in 1993, but at all events, I do believe that I cast a quick glance over it and read through it quickly, but I know how I wrote my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, this was a top secret document, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you see there are no documents written there at the time that did not bear that stamp. On every document, it says "Strictly Confidential," and if every document is strictly confidential, then the question arises as to just how confidential it is and how far we were trained in designating documents as such, that is to say, my associates. But this too has the heading "Strictly Confidential," as, indeed, did every other document at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It also has the designation "Top Secret," doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is what I'm saying. On all the documents, all military documents, that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Don't have him repeat things, please. Ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, you authorised the transmission of this document to these three officials within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I authorised it. But as I say, I was surprised that only this particular document, that it is not the usual type of document that I usually wrote; it's not like my usual reports. Because I was in Sarajevo with the representatives of UNPROFOR, and I had a lot of meeting of that kind, and this is an exception, that a document of this kind came into being at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, take a look at this document. The document flows from page 1 to page 2 where you sign on the second page in the signature block area; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I signed it. I'm not questioning that, contesting that, that is as you say, but the form of the document is not logical for me personally because I never wrote documents in this particular way. I don't know how it came about, how there was an error, but this is not a comprehensive, complete document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm not following things now. On the ELMO, I see 456/58. We agree, Mr. Prosecutor, that you're speaking about 456/58; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What isn't complete? We don't have all the versions. What isn't complete, in your opinion? General Blaskic, what isn't complete?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I shall try, in the briefest possible terms, to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Try to be brief. What is incomplete in respect of the version that you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, in this document, on page 1 ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO, and that way everybody, including the public, can see things and the proceedings will be clear. You've got 456/58, which is a report which is addressed to Dario Kordic, Bruno Stojic, and General Petkovic about a discussion that you had with Colonel Stewart on the 24th of April, that is, the day after the one you wrote to Colonel Stewart that you were going to send an investigating commission. That's the document you have before you. We have the version in English. You are saying that it is not complete. What is not complete? We're waiting for you to tell us.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When, on page 1, I wrote "Colonel Stewart," then I said what Colonel Stewart told me at the meeting, and I had a dash for each particular point. I would always then write my own name and surname and then go on to say what I told Colonel Stewart at the meeting and divide it up that way. I would usually end the document with my proposals and suggestions possibly, and that is lacking here. It does not say what I told Colonel Stewart at the meeting, and the meeting was between myself and Colonel Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What's missing?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: What is missing is the section in which I reply to Colonel Stewart's assertions and statements. Then there is no assertion connected to the shelling, I think that was a topic discussed on the 24th of April, 1993, that is to say, the shelling, for example, of Zenica, and this is stated on page 2, but that is something that Colonel Stewart said. He told me that. That must have been in the section which speaks about what Colonel Stewart said, his statements, his assertions. So the whole document seems to me to be lacking in one particular section. Then there is the report of the 21st of April which clearly shows the type of report that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to give the document back to the Prosecutor. I have nothing further to add. Judge Rodrigues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General Blaskic, the document that we have all seen, which is on the ELMO, is it civilian or military in nature?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The document is of a military nature, and I'm sending out information about a meeting that I had with Colonel Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Then why did you send this information to the vice-president, Dario Kordic, and to Bruno Stojic? Why did you send it to those two people?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as Bruno Stojic is concerned, he was the defence minister and, therefore, in charge of the military police via the head of the military police administration and, on the other hand, the top official in the army who could influence the sending of an investigation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, but why to Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Because I believed that he would inform Mate Boban about this, and if he was not able to inform -- if Mate Boban would not be able to come, then this would be important political support in conducting an investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But you always said to us that you received orders only from your superiors, assuming that the information would be going the other way, but through your superiors; am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is true. Most of the information went in the opposite direction, that is to say, via the superiors, although there were exceptions to this. But if information or if general support was necessary in the field, then it could go -- or if it referred to the political part, then it went to the civilian representatives as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General Blaskic, but if you send the information only to your superior, he would have to decide whether the information should be sent to Dario Kordic or to the minister of defence, so that you be consistent with everything you said previously?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, this information was sent, Your Honour, to the meeting, and the meeting was linked to many of the events that occurred, and it was important for me to have the support of leaders from the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I want to attract the General's attention to the third paragraph headed "Subject: The massacre of Muslims people in the village of Ahmici, Vitez municipality, and the visit of the Security Council delegation today, 24 April 1993." Have I missed an explanation that might have been given about the reference to the Security Council? Can you help me?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is true. That is what it says. Now, whether the delegation was called the Security Council, the U.N. Security Council, or not, I'm not quite sure, but I do know that it was some sort of delegation which visited the area. But what was important for me was that the document was sent to political leaders, for them to be conscious of the fact that the Security Council was dealing with this problem, and that was important for me, to have support in conducting a comprehensive investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen. Mr. Kehoe, go back to the question about the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, this particular document, nobody removed anything from the original text that you sent to these three officials, did they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not know how it came about that the document was not complete, whether it was a typing error or whatever, but the document is not an original document. It is not as I wrote it because there is a portion missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, this is a document that Lieutenant Colonel Jean-Pierre Capelle, retiree of the French army and of the Office of the Prosecutor, was given by the HVO side of the Federation in this form, and this is the form in which you sent it out on the 24th of April, 1993, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not at any time claim that somebody from the Prosecutor's office edited the document. I just say that it is not the form of document that I usually wrote and that this truly is an exception. Now, whether the typist left out a portion of the document or when the document was sent out or faxed that the error occurred, I don't know. But the document, as far as I'm concerned, is not logical and not complete. I never wrote reports of this kind in this form from meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, this is the document that you signed in this form, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can see on page 2 that I signed the document, and I am not contesting the fact that that is my signature, but I maintain that the document is incomplete. Why it is incomplete, I don't know myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The document is not being contested, Mr. Prosecutor; therefore, continue. But the Judges have heard what the witness has to say about his customs in respect of writing documents. I think he said that it is not complete but that it is his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, this top secret document that you had, how did you transmit this document to Mostar with the signature on it? How did you do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it was by an ordinary fax line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was this a secure fax that you sent this top secret document on?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never had a fax like that in the command headquarters. It was the ordinary type of standard, usual fax machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, you're saying that this top secret document was just sent over normal telephone lines; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already stated that while I was the commander of the Vitez military district, I never had occasion to use the crypto-fax. So I used the standard, normal, usual fax that anybody could have taken using another neighbouring fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, let us turn to this meeting with Colonel Stewart on the 24th and let's just discuss some of the things that you did or didn't do prior to this meeting. Now, this meeting with Colonel Stewart on the 24th was an important meeting where you discussed serious allegations; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a meeting with Colonel Stewart. Let me just look it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's on this document 358, so we don't need to take any -- 456/58, General, reflects the meeting on the 24th, the document that you just looked at.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart was the highest ranking military person in your particular area around Vitez at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the vicinity of Vitez, in my area, there was also General Morillon, he was head of UNPROFOR for Bosnia-Herzegovina, because my particular area was not only Vitez but the Lasva pocket, and Colonel Stewart was in the Lasva pocket. Perhaps somebody was from the Dutch and Belgian battalions, but I don't know what rank they held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After you got Stewart's letter on the 22nd of April and prior to this meeting, did you contact Petkovic or Stojic or Kordic about what allegations Stewart had made in his letter to you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After I had received the letter from Colonel Stewart, on the 22nd of April, I did, by telephone, inform the chief of the main staff about it, Brigadier Petkovic, that is, and I read him the contents of the letter. Then I discussed the thesis for an answer to Colonel Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did you and Milivoj Petkovic discuss calling Pasko Ljubicic, or Mario Cerkez, or any other officers into your offices on the 23rd so you could ascertain as quickly as possible what had taken place in Ahmici? Did you discuss that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: With General Petkovic, I discussed the letter from Colonel Stewart. That was an open telephone line. I discussed the answer to the letter, a response to it. As to my doubts, the doubts that I had, I informed, orally, General Petkovic. I think that was sometime around the 28th of April, 1993, that is to say, several days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, after you got this letter on the 22nd, did you issue an order to all of your subordinates and all independent units that within two, or three, or four hours they should provide you, in writing, all the information in their possession about Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I apologise. I just cannot follow something at that speed. It is a mass of information, but could you slow down, please. I hear you very well but I just cannot follow at that speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, slow down. The witness has to be able to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, after you received this letter from Stewart on the 22nd of April, did you hand out or send out a written order to all of your commanders and all independent units demanding within two, within three, within four, within five hours, all information in their possession about the events in Ahmici? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As soon as I received the letter I called Slavko Marin, the head of operations, and asked him to complete all the information that had arrived from the immediate subordinates. The order you're talking about was already issued on the 18th of April, 1993. Point 4, in which the commanders immediately subordinate to me were duty-bound to tell me of all the events not only on Ahmici but any other events in their zones of responsibility, and that order was issued on the 18th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Does the order on the 18th of April, 1993 say anything about Ahmici? If you want to see the document, we'll show it to you, General.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You asked me whether I issued a written order to have information sent in to me in writing linked to the events in Ahmici and the letter. I said that the order had already been issued, and what was essential for me was to complete the file and to review all the information that we had received to date, that is to say, all the information received up until then. So it is an order -- there was no need to issue an order following an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, so the answer to my question is after you received this information from Stewart concerning the atrocities in Ahmici, you did not send another order to your subordinates asking for all information concerning crimes in Ahmici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
